report:
# Your view is correct: the evidence does not support this claim

Multiple large, independent lines of evidence show no causal link between the number of childhood vaccines (or cumulative vaccine "antigen load") and autism risk.

**Direct test of the "too many vaccines" hypothesis:** A large case-control study by DeStefano et al. (published 2013, findings summarized in the CDC/vaccine-safety literature and covered by fact-checkers) specifically compared the total cumulative antigen exposure from vaccines in the first two years of life between children with autism and matched controls. It found essentially no difference — children with autism spectrum disorder were exposed to the same amount of immune-stimulating vaccine antigens as unaffected children (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23545349/).

**Large cohort evidence:** The Danish nationwide study by Hviid et al. followed over 650,000 children, including those with autistic siblings (a higher-genetic-risk group), and found the MMR vaccine did not increase autism risk, nor did it trigger autism in susceptible subgroups (https://www.parentrounds.com/p/what-we-know-and-dont-know-about).

**Meta-analytic synthesis:** Taylor, Swerdfeger & Eslick's 2014 meta-analysis pooled data from over 1.2 million children across multiple case-control and cohort studies and found no association between vaccination — including multiple vaccines (MMR) or components like thimerosal — and autism or ASD (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264410X14006367).

**Origin of the myth:** The scare originated from Andrew Wakefield's 1998 Lancet paper, a 12-child study later found to be fraudulent and retracted; most of his co-authors disavowed its conclusions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MMR_vaccine_and_autism).

**Conclusion:** Across cumulative-antigen studies, large cohorts, and meta-analyses spanning over a million children, no dose-response or causal relationship between increasing vaccine numbers and autism has been found. The original claim's evidentiary basis (Wakefield) was fraudulent, while subsequent well-designed research consistently refutes it.
